Researchers evaluated respiratory specimens from individuals presenting with acute respiratory infections to track how the circulating pathogen has evolved relative to the founding pandemic lineage. The investigation focused on determining whether mutations in the neuraminidase surface glycoprotein might compromise the inhibitory effectiveness of widely utilized antiviral drugs, including oseltamivir and zanamivir. Although the sequenced isolates displayed multiple amino acid substitutions across the neuraminidase gene, none carried the major recognized genetic markers that confer reduced drug sensitivity. The study contextualizes these genomic observations within the broader evolutionary history of the pathogen, noting that the 2009 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 pandemic caused substantial morbidity and mortality on a global scale. In the years following its initial emergence, continuous molecular surveillance has remained essential because structural changes in the viral neuraminidase gene can alter multiple biological properties. Specifically, amino acid mutations within this gene may influence the ongoing evolution of the virus, facilitate immune evasion against host defenses, and modify viral susceptibility to neuraminidase inhibitors. To assess the molecular characteristics of circulating strains during the 2023–2024 season, the authors conducted an observational surveillance protocol involving patients admitted with acute respiratory infections in Shiraz. Between November 2023 and December 2024, the team collected a total of 300 respiratory samples across the hospitalized cohort. Each specimen was systematically screened for the presence of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assays. From this initial diagnostic screening of 300 clinical samples, the researchers identified fourteen specimens that tested positive for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, providing the defined sample set for comprehensive downstream molecular and computational characterization. The fourteen confirmed positive isolates subsequently underwent full-length neuraminidase gene sequencing to identify all coding changes present across the complete viral gene. In addition to amino acid substitution analysis, the researchers conducted phylogenetic analysis, structural modeling, and computational molecular docking to evaluate how the observed sequence variations might affect viral protein structure and drug interactions. For phylogenetic comparison, the investigators utilized the historical pandemic reference strain designated A/California/07/2009 (GenBank accession NC_026434.1). Comparing the newly isolated Iranian sequences directly against this reference strain allowed the authors to measure the extent of neuraminidase sequence divergence that has accumulated relative to the founding A(H1N1)pdm09 lineage. Detailed sequence analysis of the fourteen isolates uncovered eighteen distinct amino acid substitutions distributed across the neuraminidase gene. The two most prevalent substitutions detected in the cohort were V241I and N369K, each occurring in 13 of the 14 isolates, representing a frequency of 92.9 percent. The researchers noted that V241I and N369K are consistent with previously documented lineage-associated permissive substitutions that commonly circulate in modern A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses. Among the other identified changes, the N200S substitution appeared in 4 of the 14 isolates (28.6 percent), while the V394I substitution was observed in 2 of the 14 isolates (14.3 percent). Additionally, the analysis identified the N386K substitution, which has been previously associated with the alteration of an N-linked glycosylation site on the neuraminidase protein. A central objective of the genomic evaluation was screening the fourteen neuraminidase sequences for established resistance-associated substitutions recognized by the World Health Organization. This targeted screening revealed that none of the isolates harbored major known neuraminidase inhibitor resistance markers, confirming the complete absence of the classic H275Y substitution as well as the I223V substitution. To supplement the sequence-level screening, the researchers carried out structural modeling and computational molecular docking with the antiviral agents oseltamivir and zanamivir. The docking simulations indicated preserved predicted binding of both oseltamivir and zanamivir to the viral neuraminidase active site, reinforcing the genetic findings that the analyzed viral variants maintain predicted susceptibility to these therapeutic agents. The authors concluded that while influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses isolated from hospitalized patients in Shiraz during the 2023–2024 period exhibited measurable genetic variability in the neuraminidase gene, they completely lacked established neuraminidase inhibitor resistance-associated substitutions. The sequence-based evidence confirms the absence of established resistance markers among the fourteen analyzed clinical isolates, suggesting that standard antiviral therapies retained their molecular targets during the study window. However, because this investigation was strictly observational and did not evaluate clinical trial outcomes or patient treatment responses, the researchers emphasized the necessity of continued molecular surveillance to monitor for the potential emergence of clinically relevant neuraminidase mutations in circulating populations. records.content: Diagnostic Technologies Anatomic Pathology Clinical Chemistry Digital Pathology Flow Cytometry Hematology & Serology Immunoassay Mass Spectrometry Microbiology Molecular Diagnostics Point-of-Care Urinalysis & Toxicology Lab Products Biochemicals & Chemical Reagents Information Technology Lab Automation Lab Equipment Lab Safety Labware & Consumables Quality Systems Disease States Allergy & Autoimmune Cancer Cardiovascular Cerebrovascular Dementias & Alzheimer’s Diabetes & Metabolic Diseases Infectious Diseases Kidney Disease Respiratory Disease Sepsis Womens Health Lab Management Accreditation Company News Compliance Proficiency Testing Resource Center Resources Podcasts Webcasts White Papers Videos Comparison Guides Edition Archive Select Page Flu Test Positivity Tops 10% Nationwide Nov 16, 2026 | Flu & Respiratory Infections | The CDC’s latest weekly influenza surveillance report shows activity rising across much of the US, with H1N1 continuing to dominate and hospitalizations increasing. Seasonal influenza activity is increasing in many parts of the US and is higher than typically observed at this time of year, according to the CDC’s latest weekly surveillance report for Week 44, which ended Nov 7. Clinical laboratories nationwide tested 52,287 specimens during the week, and 5,911 (11.3%) were positive for influenza. Flu test positivity rose nationally and in eight of the 10 US Department of Health and Human Services regions. It remained stable in Region 8 and declined in Region 9, which the CDC attributes to possibly incomplete reporting. Since Oct 4 (Week 40), clinical labs have tested 309,131 specimens, with 24,324 (7.9%) testing positive. Influenza A accounted for 99.2% of positive specimens in Week 44. The CDC cautioned that an earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak or greater overall severity. Its preliminary in-season assessment classifies severity as low across all age groups, though the agency noted the assessment may change as activity climbs. H1N1 Predominates, With Growing Genetic Diversity Public health laboratories reported 680 positive influenza viruses in Week 44, of which 670 were influenza A and 10 were influenza B. Of the 460 influenza A viruses subtyped, 455 (98.9%) were A(H1N1)pdm09 and 5 (1.1%) were A(H3N2). Since Week 21 (the week ending May 30), 83.4% of reported influenza A viruses have been A(H1N1)pdm09, most of them in the D.3.1.1 HA subclade. The CDC noted that recently circulating D.3.1.1 viruses have divided into distinct groups with different genetic changes in their HA genes, and that there is more genetic diversity among co-circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses than previously seen. The agency said it is too early to know which viruses may predominate or whether there could be implications for vaccine effectiveness this season. Of the 764 influenza viruses genetically characterized since May 24, 555 were A(H1N1)pdm09, and 554 of those (99.8%) belonged to the D.3.1.1 subclade. Among 109 A(H3N2) viruses, 104 (95.4%) were subclade K. The 100 B/Victoria viruses were spread across several subclades, led by C.5.6.1 (48.0%) and C.3.1 (40.0%). Vaccine Match and Antiviral Susceptibility Antigenic testing showed most circulating viruses are well recognized by antisera to the 2026-2027 vaccine reference viruses. Of 147 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses characterized by hemagglutination inhibition, 140 (95.2%) were well recognized by antisera to the A/Missouri/11/2025-like reference virus. All 35 A(H3N2) viruses and all 33 B/Victoria viruses tested were well recognized by antisera to their respective vaccine reference viruses. For antiviral susceptibility, the CDC tested 758 viruses collected since May 24 against oseltamivir, peramivir, and zanamivir, and 725 against baloxavir. Eight A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses (1.1% of all viruses tested) showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir and carried the NA-I223V and NA-S247N substitutions. No viruses showed reduced inhibition by peramivir or zanamivir, and none showed decreased susceptibility to baloxavir. Outpatient, Hospital, and Mortality Indicators Outpatient respiratory illness is above baseline. Nationally, 3.2% of ILINet patient visits were for influenza-like illness in Week 44, above the national baseline of 2.9%. Emergency department visits with a discharge diagnosis of influenza reached 2.2%, and the percentage rose in every HHS region except Region 7, where it was stable. The CDC’s ILI activity map shows one jurisdiction at a very high level, six at a high level, and nine at a moderate level. Hospitalization data point to rising severe disease, particularly among older adults. Hospitals reported 9,584 laboratory-confirmed, influenza-associated admissions to the National Healthcare Safety Network in Week 44, a rate of 2.8 per 100,000 population. FluSurv-NET recorded 3,262 laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalizations between Oct. 4 and Nov. 7, for a cumulative rate of 8.7 per 100,000. The highest rate was among adults 65 and older, at 28.0 per 100,000. Influenza accounted for 0.4% of deaths in Week 44, a stable figure that has trended upward over the past eight weeks. The CDC received reports of two pediatric deaths from the current season this week, bringing the season total to five. One death from the 2025-2026 season was also reported, raising that season’s pediatric death total to 203. The CDC estimates that at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations, and 2,100 deaths have been associated with flu so far this season. Its FluSight forecasts predict a likely national increase in flu hospital admissions, ranging from 8,300 to 34,400, for the week ending Nov. 28. They also predict that 1.8% to 7.7% of emergency department visits will be due to flu. Novel Influenza Surveillance No new confirmed human infections with a novel influenza virus were reported to the CDC as of Nov 7. Public health laboratories have detected four H5-positive specimens since Oct 4, none of them in Week 44. The CDC noted that these figures reflect specimens tested rather than human cases. The CDC continues to recommend annual influenza vaccination for everyone 6 months and older and says prescription antivirals should be started as early as possible, especially for patients at higher risk of complications. All data are preliminary and may change as more reports are received.
